name: live-status-line
title: Live Status Line
description: A single line saying what an agent is doing right now — the status bar of an agent run. Takes a `state` from Agent Presence's vocabulary, a `status` describing the current micro-action, an optional `detail` naming what the action is acting on (a filename, a query, a table), an optional `startedAt` that drives a live elapsed counter, and an `onCancel` shown whenever the agent is active. It replaces rather than accumulates, which is the whole distinction from its neighbours: Reasoning Stream keeps a scrollable trace, Chain-of-Thought Timeline keeps the entire turn's history, and this keeps exactly one thing — which is what makes it cheap enough to leave in permanent product chrome like a toolbar, sidebar footer, or table row. Composes Agent Presence in its `line` form for the indicator rather than reimplementing one, so the turn-taking grammar (motion means the machine is busy, stillness means it's your turn) holds here automatically. The status text is keyed so React's reconciliation runs its swap animation exactly once per real change; a re-render with unchanged text never re-animates. Layout is deliberately stable: the row holds a minimum height so changing text length cannot reflow its container, and the detail truncates before the verb does so 'Reading' stays legible even when the filename cannot. Unlike most components in this system the elapsed counter ticks internally rather than being caller-owned, because forcing a re-render once a second for a display detail would be a poor API. Use it wherever an agent's current activity should be visible without dedicating a panel to it. Not for the reasoning text itself (use Reasoning Stream), not for a per-artifact generation progress surface (use Generation Placeholder), and not as a general toast or notification.
docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`, the `pd-status-swap` keyframe from @pixeldosa/pixeldosa-theme, and @pixeldosa/agent-presence, which it composes for the indicator. Installing this pulls Agent Presence in automatically.

meta.engineeringNotes: The defining constraint is that this component replaces rather than accumulates. Accumulation is what makes agent activity surfaces expensive — a growing list needs scroll management, virtualisation at length, and a decision about when to collapse. Holding exactly one line keeps it cheap enough to live permanently in product chrome, and pushes the history question to Reasoning Stream and Chain-of-Thought Timeline where it belongs. It composes Agent Presence's `line` form rather than drawing its own dots, which is the system's compose-don't-reinvent rule applied where it genuinely fits: the turn-taking grammar then holds here for free, including the fact that a `suggesting` or `awaitingApproval` status stops moving. Two layout decisions prevent the jitter this pattern usually has: a minimum row height, so text of varying length cannot reflow the container around it, and truncation applied to the detail rather than the verb, so 'Reading' remains legible when a long filename cannot be. The elapsed counter is the one place this system deliberately breaks its own 'the caller owns async state' convention — every other component takes progress, busy and duration as props — because a live counter would otherwise force the consumer to re-render once a second purely for a display detail. The interval is only started while the agent is actually active, and never when no `startedAt` was supplied.
meta.motionNotes: One animation, and it maps to one state change: when the status text is replaced, the new text fades up three pixels over `--pd-duration-fast` with `--pd-ease-decelerate`. Short deliberately — micro-actions can change every second or two, and anything longer would read as churn rather than as replacement. It is keyed on the status string so React's reconciliation fires it exactly once per genuine change; an unchanged status that re-renders does not re-animate, which is the same mechanism Progressive Reveal and Reasoning Stream use. The indicator's own motion is inherited from Agent Presence and is not duplicated here. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the swap is dropped entirely: text simply changes, which loses nothing, because the information was always the words rather than the transition between them.
